title: HKDM script tensor: seed data
note: Compiled on 2026-10-03 from the reference pages listed with each script and record, cross-checked the same day against Omniglot where it has a page. Basis 'source' means the script, substrate and start year are stated on a listed page (end years may be approximate, as each note says); basis 'general' means general knowledge not yet checked against a page. Every record still needs review by an epigraphist before it is cited.

scripts.name: Arabic
scripts.region: Arabia, then West Asia and beyond

records.note: First documents in the Uruk IV period, c. 3300 BCE, written in vertical columns until the signs were rotated c. 2294–2270 BCE.
After the rotation, horizontal left to right. Latest firmly dateable tablet: Uruk, 79/80 CE.
The vertical style stayed on monumental stone stelae until the middle of the 2nd millennium BCE.
Logo-consonantal. Right to left was preferred. Last known inscription: the Graffito of Esmet-Akhom at Philae, 394 CE.
Left to right also occurs; the way the signs face shows the reading order.
Boustrophedon is attested.
Cursive hieroglyphs on papyrus for religious literature (material from the source; the date range is general knowledge).
Cursive hieroglyphs on wood (material from the source; the date range is general knowledge).
Stamp seals (soapstone). Predominantly right to left: signs are compressed on the left, as if the writer ran out of space.
Pottery inscriptions and clay seal impressions from c. 2800–2600 BCE onward; terracotta.
Copper plates, tools and weapons.
Some boustrophedon examples.
Oracle bone inscriptions, Late Shang, c. 1250–1050 BCE. Morphosyllabic. Columns top to bottom, ordered right to left.
Bronze inscriptions from the Late Shang (c. 1250 BCE), at their height in the Western Zhou, continuing through the Qin and Han; vertical columns, top to bottom.
Earliest surviving slips from the 5th century BCE; the standard medium in the Han; largely abandoned by the 4th century CE. Written vertically, right to left.
The Chu Silk Manuscript, c. 300 BCE; the Mawangdui silk texts, 168 BCE. Silk and bamboo were the two book media of the period (the span covers these two finds).
Paper as a writing medium from the 1st century CE; vertical columns until the 20th century.
Horizontal left to right became predominant in the 20th century.
c. 1050–146 BCE. Oldest inscription: the Ahiram sarcophagus, Byblos, c. 1000 BCE. The first script with a fixed writing direction.
800 BCE to 600 CE; the written medium of the Persian empire from c. 500 BCE.
Thirty Imperial Aramaic documents on leather from Bactria (probably Balkh), dated 353–324 BCE (Khalili Collection).
Oldest substantial inscriptions c. 740/730 BCE (Dipylon vase, cup of Nestor). Originally mostly right to left, like Phoenician.
For a time boustrophedon was common (the source states the practice; the date range is general knowledge).
Left to right became the norm in the classical period.
Edicts of Ashoka at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra. Developed in Gandhara between the 5th and 3rd centuries BCE.
Gandharan Buddhist texts on birch bark from the 1st century CE.
Wooden tablets from Niya, 3rd century CE.
Some evidence that it survived until the 7th century in Khotan and Niya.
Earliest indisputably dated: the rock edicts of Ashoka, c. 250–232 BCE. Usually left to right.
Potsherds from Anuradhapura dated 6th to early 4th century BCE; controversial (Falk questions some readings).
Metal plates and coins are among the attested surfaces (the date range follows the stone record).
An early coin from Eran runs right to left, as in Aramaic (the fact is from the source; its date is general knowledge).
Cave entrances and stone beds; dated 3rd century BCE to 1st century CE. Adds signs for ṉ ṟ ṛ ḷ.
Potsherds and jar burials.
Earlier dates (5th–4th century BCE) proposed from Sri Lankan finds; contested.
Allahabad pillar inscription c. 350 CE; sometimes called Late Brahmi.
Iron pillars and Gupta gold coins (Bayana hoard).
Pallava script from the 4th century CE; Grantha on temple inscriptions; still used in religious contexts.
Some of the earliest authenticated copper plates were issued by Pallava kings in the 4th century; copper plates stayed the main legal record for centuries (the end year is approximate).
Palm leaves (material from the source; the date range is general knowledge).
From the Gupta script in the late 6th century; the main script of North India by the 7th; replaced by Nagari by about the 11th.
Copper-plate land grants (tāmra-paṭṭa).
Palm-leaf sutras. The Hōryū-ji Heart Sutra, 7th–8th century, may be the earliest extant Sanskrit manuscript of that text.
Brought to Japan by Kūkai in 806; written with a brush in Shingon, Tendai and Shugendō to this day.
Developed in the second half of the 8th century; earliest known inscription 774 CE (Omniglot); widespread in Kashmir and the north-west until the 12th century; last known inscription 1204 CE.
In Kashmir, books were written on birch bark until the 16th century (Wikipedia, Birch bark manuscript). The start follows Sharada's 8th-century start.

Wikipedia's Birch bark manuscript page calls the Bakhshali manuscript (estimated 2nd–3rd century) and the Gilgit manuscripts (5th–6th century) Śāradā script. This conflicts with Sharada's 8th-century start on the Sharada page and on Omniglot; their early scripts are often classed as predecessors.
Nāgarī variants recognisably close to Devanāgarī are attested from the 1st-century Rudradaman inscriptions (an early-development claim).
In regular use by the 7th century; early Devanāgarī in the Kutila inscription, 992 CE; modern form by about 1000 CE.
An inscribed brick from Uttar Pradesh, 1217 CE (British Museum).
Copper-plate grants (general knowledge).
Palm-leaf manuscripts (general knowledge).
Paper is attested in India from the second half of the 7th century (Wikipedia, Paper history); its use for Devanagari from about 1300 is general knowledge, not yet checked.
Announced 1443–44, published 1446 (Hunminjeongeum). Columns top to bottom, right to left. Whether it is 'featural' is debated.
Horizontal left to right dominant since the 20th century. 'Featural' is debated.

Cuneiform was also written on wax-coated wooden boards (Omniglot). Writing boards were in use in Mesopotamia in the 1st millennium BCE; ivory boards from Nimrud, 8th century BCE (Wikipedia, Wax tablet). Direction follows the clay records.

Rock carvings, statuettes, stelae and a sphinx at Serabit el-Khadim; road-side rock at Wadi el-Hol. Mixed directions. Dated mid-19th (early date) to mid-16th century BCE (late date); the date is debated. Acrophonic letters adapted from Egyptian signs.
Old Latin could be written right to left, as Etruscan and early Greek were. Earliest Latin inscriptions 6th century BCE (Omniglot).
Old Latin could also be written boustrophedon.
From the middle Republic on, almost always left to right (the start year is approximate).
Paper mills in Europe from Xàtiva, Spain, 1056, then Italy in the 13th century; later print.
First known text in the Arabic alphabet: the Zabad inscription, 512 CE. From Nabataean Aramaic; the an-Namāra inscription (328 CE) is still Nabataean script, with letter joining.
The Birmingham Qur'an manuscript, Hijazi script on parchment, radiocarbon dated 568–645 CE (the date of the skin, not necessarily of the writing; the end year is approximate).
Paper reached Samarkand in 751 and Baghdad had paper mills by 794–795.
Paper reached Tibet around the mid-7th century; pecha books moved from palm leaf to birch bark to paper. The script was finalized in the 630s or 640s.

Bilingual coins: Greek on the obverse, Kharoshthi Prakrit on the reverse, issued by Indo-Greek kings from Apollodotus I (c. 180 BCE); the kingdom lasted to about 10 CE. The first bilingual coins (Pantaleon, Agathocles) used Brahmi.
Documents on leather from Niya (general knowledge; the pages opened mention only wood for Niya).
The first Indo-Greek bilingual coins, of Pantaleon and Agathocles (c. 185–170 BCE), carry Brahmi legends.
In East Asia Siddham was usually written left to right, but occasionally in the Chinese manner, top to bottom in columns (Wikipedia, Siddhaṃ script).

Buddhist texts carried to China along the Silk Road were written in Siddham; supply to Japan was cut by the purges of foreign religions in the mid-9th century (source). The substrate and start are general knowledge.
Inscriptions on stone relic caskets (and a crystal casket) at Bhattiprolu, 3rd–1st century BCE. gh, j, m, l and s differ radically from Ashokan Brahmi; the inherent vowel is discarded.
Under the Kadamba dynasty (325–550) Brahmi became shorter and rounder; distinct by the 5th century; evolved into Telugu-Kannada by the 10th.
Copper-plate inscriptions in Kadamba script.
Used between the 7th and 11th centuries on copper plates; Telugu and Kannada separated between 1100 and 1400.
Based on Brahmi; developed c. 3rd–5th century; stone monuments were the main medium, in South India and Southeast Asia (Omniglot).
Some of the earliest authenticated copper plates were issued by Pallava kings in the 4th century.

The Chola-Pallava script replaced Vaṭṭeḻuttu in the north from the 8th century and evolved into modern Tamil. Palm leaves were the main medium; scribes avoided piercing them, so the puḷḷi fell out of regular use.
Earliest form in the 12th-century Vaishikatantram; systematised by the 13th; current form 16th century from Vaṭṭeḻuttu, Kolezhuttu and Grantha (source). The palm-leaf substrate is general knowledge.
Medieval Sinhala emerged around 750 CE; written on dried palm leaves, which split along straight lines, so round shapes were preferred.
Royal documents on stone until the fall of the Kandyan Kingdom in 1815.
Current from the 10th to the 14th century; the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā in ink on palm leaves.
Silver coins of the Harikela kingdom.
Differentiated from Gaudi in the 14th–15th centuries; first significant typeset book 1778 (source). Paper before print is general knowledge. Also the official script for Meitei (Manipuri).
Modern form from the 14th century, when palm-leaf manuscript culture became dominant; Wikipedia attributes the curved tops to palm leaves tearing along straight lines.

Earliest known manuscript: Adi Parva, 1591–92; the headline was abandoned in the 17th–19th centuries, when it was the bankers', merchants' and traders' script (source). The substrate is general knowledge.
Evolved from Sharada in the 10th century as mercantile shorthand in Punjab and Sindh, often without full vowels (source). The substrate and end are general knowledge.
Proto-Gurmukhi writing c. 1470–1490 on the tomb of Rae Feroze.
Standardized by Guru Angad around 1530–1535; manuscripts since the 1500s.

First known from 6th-century coins and copper plates (reign of Ura Konthouba, c. 568–653); in use until the early 18th century, when Bengali script replaced it. Scholars disagree significantly on when it developed.
A modernised version approved for schools in 1980; in Unicode since 2009.
Designed by the Tibetan monk ʼPhags-pa in 1269 for Kublai Khan; written vertically, columns left to right; used for about a century under the Yuan (a Christian tombstone at Quanzhou, 1314).
Seals and currency.
Earliest: the Kesongo stone, 763 CE; stone inscriptions form the bulk of the corpus, to the 16th century.
Plates and foils of lead-bronze, copper and gold.
Everyday writing on palm leaf (lontar); the Tanjung Tanah manuscript, 1379–1387.
Evolved from Kawi in the 14th–15th centuries; lontar palm leaves.
Daluang (local paper) in the 16th–17th centuries, European paper dominant by the 19th.
Traditionally written on palm leaves with a stylus or on bamboo with a knife (source); the date range is general knowledge.
Oldest dated documents 1591 and 1599 (Archivo General de Indias); the Doctrina Christiana printed in 1593; ink on paper in the Spanish period.
Adapted from Pallava; oldest dated Khmer inscription, Angkor Borei, 611 CE; stelae throughout the former Khmer Empire.
Palm-leaf manuscripts in the Khom style (source mentions them; the date range is general knowledge).

From Old Khmer via Sukhothai; traditionally dated 1283. The Ram Khamhaeng inscription (1292) is questioned by many scholars; some date the earliest Thai to 1219 (source). Stone as substrate is general knowledge.
Earliest evidence 1035 (an 18th-century casting of an older inscription points to 984); square forms because petroglyphs were a main medium.
Rounded cursive forms from the 17th century with wider use of palm leaves, which a stylus would rip with straight lines.
Folded paper books (parabaik) from the 17th century.

lineage.note: Wikipedia: a clear dependency on Aramaic with extensive modifications. Omniglot: 'possibly' derived from Aramaic.
The leading hypothesis, not settled for lack of direct evidence.
A minority hypothesis; the evidence is called insufficient.
Sources differ: Wikipedia (Gupta script) says Siddham produced Devanagari; Omniglot derives Devanagari from Nāgarī, an eastern Gupta variant, which later replaced Siddham.
Omniglot's account; see the Siddham link for the other.
Late Gupta script of Nepal and North India is the most likely model.
Mauryan Brahmi travelled to Bhattiprolu soon after the 3rd century BCE; Salomon suggests it was first made for a Dravidian language.
Vaṭṭeḻuttu was replaced in the north by Chola-Pallava from the 8th century; its share in modern Tamil is partial.
With Vaṭṭeḻuttu and Kolezhuttu in its 16th-century form.
Medieval Sinhala (c. 750) is thought to derive from Grantha.
Possibly via Buginese; Scott favours a South Sulawesi ancestor (Old Makassar); Wade points to Cham.
From Pyu, Old Mon, or directly from a South Indian script (Kadamba or Pallava).
A Brahmic abugida of the Gupta lineage; its origins and date are debated.
